items.prompt: What is an objection?
choices: A final decision the buyer can never revisit later
A stated reason for holding back right now
A request for a discount made by the buyer
items.explanation: An objection is a stated reason for holding back at this moment, not a final verdict.

items.prompt: How did Rep B treat the objection?
choices: As a wall that had to be pushed through
As a signal that the call should end
As a request for more information
items.explanation: Rep B asked what still cost time, treating the line as the start of an answer.

items.prompt: What did Rep A do after hearing the objection?
choices: Argued that the incumbent is worse
Asked what still cost the buyer time
Offered a lower price right away
items.explanation: Rep A walked through feature comparisons, which made the buyer defend the choice.

items.prompt: What do people often do when a decision of theirs is attacked?
choices: Reconsider it quietly and calmly
Defend it more strongly than before
Ask for a longer demo first
items.explanation: People protect decisions they have already made, so attacking one hardens it.

items.prompt: How long did Rep B take to uncover a real problem?
choices: The full ten minutes of the call
After a discount
About thirty seconds in
items.explanation: The story contrasts Rep A's ten minutes with Rep B's half minute of one good question.

items.prompt: How often do objections come up on a typical deal?
choices: Almost every time, in some form
Only when the price is quite high
Rarely, as long as the pitch is good
items.explanation: The unit is about what to say when they land, because they always do.

items.prompt: Is asking to understand an objection honest or manipulative?
choices: Manipulative, since it hides the rep's goal
Honest, since it aims to learn what is true
Neutral, since it changes nothing about intent
items.explanation: Asking about the buyer's real situation is the opposite of a trick.

items.prompt: Which opener treats the objection as a request for information?
choices: "Let me explain why you're wrong about this."
"Everyone says that at the start of a deal."
"That's fair. What still costs you time?"
items.explanation: Only the first acknowledges the point and asks for more information.

items.prompt: A buyer says "we already have something that works." Reply one is a ten-minute feature comparison. Reply two is a short agreement plus a question about what still costs time. Which prediction is best?
choices: Reply two, since it lets the buyer describe a problem
Reply one, since more facts outweigh a buyer's habit
Neither, since the buyer's mind was made up before the call
Reply two, but only if followed by an instant discount
items.explanation: Facts delivered against a decision make the buyer defend it, while an open question lets the buyer raise a cost of their own.
items.reference:
Wall or request?
🧱 Wall: push against it, the buyer defends harder
🔎 Request: ask, the buyer supplies the real reasons
Same objection, same product, different first ten seconds
Why: an objection is the buyer's compressed first answer, so it carries information you have not heard yet.
items.learnMore:
An objection is information, not a verdict

People defend a decision harder when it is attacked. A reply that asks what still costs time or money invites the buyer to describe their situation instead of guarding their position.

Common mistake

Hearing "we already have something" and answering with a feature comparison.
items.reflection: Think of a time someone pushed back on your idea. Did they sound like they were closing a door or giving you a clue, and which did you respond to?

items.prompt: Why does the method fail if a rep acknowledges the buyer but plans to ignore whatever answer comes back?
choices: Acknowledging an objection concedes the point for good
Buyers never answer questions about their current setup honestly at all
The aim is to learn what is true, and ignoring the answer defeats it
The answer is always a complaint about price, so nothing is lost
items.explanation: The method only works as a real question. If the answer cannot change the rep's course, it is a script, not information gathering.

🔎 Request: ask, the buyer supplies the real reasons

items.prompt: After an objection the buyer goes quiet and says "we'll keep you in mind." What most likely happened earlier in the call?
choices: The rep argued against the buyer's choice, leaving nothing to explore
The rep asked a question and the buyer ran out of answers
The rep conceded a discount that was slightly too small to matter at all
The rep agreed with everything the buyer said and ended the call early
items.explanation: A polite exit tends to follow a rep who pushed against the choice instead of opening up what is not working.

items.prompt: What is status quo bias?
choices: Choosing the newest option available on the market every time
Always picking the cheapest option on offer to the buyer
Preferring what is in place because its flaws are known
items.explanation: The familiar system's problems feel survivable, the new one's feel unknown.

items.prompt: "We already have something that works" is often really about what?
choices: The familiar system's flaws feeling survivable
The buyer having no budget approved this year
The buyer disliking the rep personally
items.explanation: The line usually protects a known setup from the cost of switching.

items.prompt: A price objection has two common causes. What are they?
choices: A dated logo, or a poor looking website
A real budget limit, or a value case that has not landed
Late delivery, or slow customer support
items.explanation: The number may be out of reach, or the buyer may not yet see its worth.

items.prompt: Should every "too expensive" get an instant discount?
choices: Yes, because a discount always closes the gap
Yes, but never more than five percent
No, ask which cause it is first
items.explanation: A discount fixes only the budget cause, and sometimes not even that.

items.prompt: What reveals the real blocker behind an objection?
choices: A direct, specific question
A longer, fuller pitch
A bigger discount offered early
items.explanation: Only asking separates the stated reason from the true one.

items.prompt: Are the stated objection and the real blocker always the same?
choices: Yes, buyers say exactly what they mean
No, they often turn out to differ
Yes, except when the topic is price
items.explanation: That gap is why the unit teaches asking before responding.

items.prompt: Which line asks about the fork in a price objection?
choices: "Would 10% off help you decide today?"
"Everyone finds it pricey at first, you know, so try it."
"Is the number outside budget, or not yet worth it?"
items.explanation: Only the first separates a budget ceiling from a value gap.

items.prompt: Which line asks about a hidden cost in the incumbent?
choices: "Does it still cost you time?"
"Isn't it getting outdated?"
"You will switch at some point anyway."
items.explanation: An open question about cost invites the buyer to name the gap themselves.

items.prompt: Two buyers both say "it's too expensive." Buyer one has $18,000 approved against a $24,000 list. Buyer two has $30,000 approved but has not seen the product work. Which pairing of replies fits?
choices: Discount both buyers by the same amount, to stay fair to each
Trade terms for buyer one, build the value case for buyer two
Walk away from buyer one, and give buyer two a small discount
Show buyer one more features, give buyer two a lower price
items.explanation: Buyer one has a real ceiling and needs a trade; buyer two has room but lacks evidence of value, so a discount would fix nothing.
items.reference:
Two objections, each with a fork
💰 "Too expensive": a real budget ceiling, or a value case that has not landed
🛋️ "We already have something": the old system's flaws feel survivable
❓ Only a question tells which one this buyer has
Why: the stated reason and the real blocker are often different things, and a wrong guess spends the whole conversation on the wrong one.
items.learnMore:
Status quo bias and the price fork

Status quo bias means the known system's problems feel survivable and the new option's problems feel unknown. A price objection hides a similar fork: the number may be outside budget, or the buyer may not yet see enough value to justify it.

Common mistake

Discounting immediately on "too expensive" without asking which fork it is.
items.reflection: Recall the last time you said "too expensive" or "I'm fine as is." What was the real reason, and would a good question have found it?

items.prompt: A rep hears "we already have something that works" and replies with a list of the incumbent's missing features. What is the main flaw?
choices: It gives too little product detail for the buyer to compare fairly
It reveals the price of the product long before it was asked for
It should have listed the features in a different order, shortest first
It argues a decision rather than finding the cost the buyer feels
items.explanation: The buyer's own description of what still costs time persuades more than a rep's list, and the list triggers defence.

items.prompt: A buyer says "too expensive", then admits the number is fine but he cannot justify it to his director. What is the real blocker?
choices: A hard budget ceiling that no trade or reasoning can move
A case his director can accept, which is an approval issue
A defect in the way the product has been priced and packaged
A misunderstanding of the list price on the written quote
items.explanation: The money exists; what is missing is an argument the decision-maker will accept, so the next step is a concrete summary for the director.

items.prompt: What is concession trading?
choices: Giving something up only in exchange for something back
Giving the buyer whatever they happen to ask for in the talks
Refusing every single change to the price
items.explanation: Each give is matched by a get, so the deal stays balanced.

items.prompt: Which is a reasonable thing to ask for in return for a discount?
choices: A shorter contract term with an early exit
A longer contract term
A smaller first order than planned
items.explanation: A longer term gives the seller more certainty in return for the lower price.

items.prompt: What does an unprompted discount signal to a buyer?
choices: The seller values this deal more highly than the buyer does
The product has just been improved by the team
The original price was never really firm
items.explanation: Giving instantly shows the number was soft.

items.prompt: What is anchoring?
choices: The first number said pulls the talk toward it
Setting the price at the lowest level possible
Writing the price down on a quote
items.explanation: The opening number frames what feels reasonable afterwards.

items.prompt: Can walking away from a deal be a good outcome?
choices: No, any deal is better than none at all
Yes, when it would cost more than it is worth
Only if the buyer asks the seller to leave
items.explanation: Not every objection resolves into a deal worth doing.

items.prompt: Which return item can help with other deals later?
choices: A longer payment delay for the buyer
A smaller scope
A reference call
items.explanation: A reference is a sales asset for the next prospects.

items.prompt: What does a reply with reasoning do to an opening number?
choices: It resets the frame instead of only haggling down
It guarantees that the buyer will agree to it
It hides the seller's own number from view for good
items.explanation: A counter with reasons stands on its own, not on the buyer's number.

items.prompt: Who benefits from a trade rather than a giveaway?
choices: Only the seller, who keeps more margin
Both sides, since each sees what they get
Only the buyer, who gets more choices
items.explanation: The trade is explicit, so both can judge whether it is fair.

items.prompt: A buyer asks for 15% off. Rep one agrees at once. Rep two says yes if the contract term doubles. What is the main difference by the next renewal?
choices: There is none, since both reach the same discount in the end
Rep two's buyer will refuse to renew because of the longer term
Rep one's price is treated as soft, rep two's as a priced exchange
Rep one gets a longer term automatically as a thank-you from the buyer
items.explanation: An unconditional discount teaches that asking works; a conditional one links price to something the seller wanted.
items.reference:
A trade, not a giveaway
↗ Give: a discount, a concession
↙ Get: a longer term, a reference, faster payment
No return, no concession
Why: a one-way discount teaches the buyer that the original price was never real.
items.learnMore:
Concession trading and anchoring

A concession exchanged for something of value keeps the deal a trade. The first number said also pulls the conversation toward it, so the opening number matters.

Common mistake

Offering a discount unprompted, with nothing asked in return.
items.reflection: Think of a time you gave something up in a negotiation. What did you get back, and would you ask for something different now?

items.prompt: Why might the best reply to "can you do 20% off?" be a number with reasoning rather than a smaller discount?
choices: A reasoned counter sets a new frame instead of haggling from their anchor
Buyers never accept an offer unless a long reason comes with it
A seller must always refuse the first ask in every negotiation they ever run
A smaller discount is not permitted under most company sales policies
items.explanation: Answering with a smaller discount accepts the buyer's number as the reference; reasoning about value moves the talk elsewhere.

items.prompt: A requested concession would make the deal unprofitable and set a precedent for other customers. What is the best choice?
choices: Accept it anyway, since any deal is better than none at all
Accept it, but keep the new terms hidden from other customers
Decline politely and leave the relationship open for later
Delay replying for weeks until the buyer loses interest in asking
items.explanation: Some deals cost more than they are worth, and declining politely keeps a future one possible.

items.prompt: What is the first step after an objection lands?
choices: Reframe it
Offer a discount to soften it
Acknowledge it
items.explanation: Validating the point earns the trust needed for the next question.

items.prompt: What does isolate check?
choices: Whether this is the only blocker or one of several
Whether the buyer is telling the whole truth
Whether the rep should leave the call now
items.explanation: Solving one objection may not unblock a decision if another remains.

items.prompt: What does a reframe use to respond?
choices: A scripted rebuttal learned in advance
A fact, a number or a different angle
A larger discount than first offered
items.explanation: Reframe is substance matched to the real concern.

items.prompt: What do arguing and caving both skip?
choices: Greeting the buyer
Closing the call
Acknowledging and isolating
items.explanation: Both react to the surface line before learning what lies underneath.

items.prompt: Why does acknowledging help?
choices: Buyers defend less once heard
It ends the objection immediately and for good
It commits the buyer to buy right away
items.explanation: Showing you heard a person, not a wall, lowers the defence.

items.prompt: Is isolate meant to trap the buyer into a yes?
choices: Yes, since it forces an early commitment
No, it is a genuine question to learn the truth
Yes, but only when the topic is price
items.explanation: Used as a trap it becomes pressure, and buyers stop answering honestly.

items.prompt: If isolate finds something else is blocking, what comes next?
choices: Repeat the pitch with more energy
Offer a discount to cover everything
Address that blocker before re-pitching
items.explanation: The real blocker must be dealt with first.

items.prompt: For a price objection, a reframe often connects price to what?
choices: A number the buyer already tracks
A competitor's logo on the slide
A rep's monthly sales commission
items.explanation: Tying price to a known cost makes the value visible.

items.prompt: A buyer says "we need to think about it." Which reply follows acknowledge and isolate?
choices: "Sure, I'll check back next week to see where you have got to."
"Don't wait too long, as the price is going up this coming Friday."
"Is it because of what our competitor is offering you right now?"
"Of course. What do you want to think through, so I can help?"
items.explanation: The strong reply validates the pause and asks a specific question; the others wait passively, add pressure or guess.
items.reference:
Three steps, in this order
1. Acknowledge: validate the objection as reasonable
2. Isolate: the only blocker, or one of several?
3. Reframe: answer the real concern with substance
Both bad reflexes (argue, cave) skip steps 1 and 2
Why: arguing or caving at once responds to the surface line before you know what is underneath it.
items.learnMore:
The ten seconds that decide the call

Acknowledge earns trust, isolate finds the true blocker, and reframe answers it with a fact, number or angle rather than a script. Isolate is a real question, not a trap to extract a yes.

Common mistake

Using "if I fix X, will you sign today?" to corner the buyer. It is pressure, not isolation.
items.reflection: Think of a conversation where you rushed to answer an objection. Which of the three steps would have changed what you heard?

items.prompt: A rep isolates and learns the price concern is real, but the buyer also quietly doubts the product fits. What should happen next?
choices: Offer a discount that is meant to cover both of the issues
Address the doubt about product fit before negotiating the price
End the call and follow up with the buyer again in a month
Repeat the pitch again with an even longer list of product features
items.explanation: Solving the stated blocker alone would not move the decision, which is exactly what isolate is there to find out.

items.prompt: Which behaviour turns isolate into manipulation?
choices: Asking whether price is the only thing standing in the way
Asking what would need to be true for a go-ahead decision
Asking which part of the setup still costs the most time
Asking "if I fix this, will you sign today?"
items.explanation: A forced commitment uses isolate as pressure, while the other questions seek facts the buyer is free to answer.

items.prompt: Which is a weak reply to "it's too expensive"?
choices: "I can knock 10% off."
"Is the number outside budget?"
"What would justify it for you?"
items.explanation: An instant discount treats the objection as literal and unexamined.

items.prompt: Which is a strong reply to "we already have something that works"?
choices: "We beat it on every single feature."
"Does anything still cost you time?"
"You will outgrow it within a year."
items.explanation: The question validates and opens a door to the real cost.

items.prompt: What is wrong with "No problem, just following up" after "we need to think"?
choices: It is far too polite for a sales call
It is far too pushy for a sales call
It waits passively and finds out nothing
items.explanation: Silence after a stall leaves the real concern unknown.

items.prompt: What does the strong column never do?
choices: Argue the buyer out of their position
Ask the buyer a specific question
Use the same words the buyer used
items.explanation: It validates, then asks, instead of fighting the stated reason.

items.prompt: Why ask "is timing the only thing in the way?"
choices: It pushes the buyer to sign right away
It checks whether timing hides another blocker
It sets a firm deadline for the decision
items.explanation: Timing can cover for budget or buy-in issues.

items.prompt: "When would be better?" treats the conversation as what?
choices: A pricing problem to be solved now
A feature problem to be solved now
A scheduling problem
items.explanation: It accepts the stated reason and only moves the date.

items.prompt: After the strong question is answered, what comes next?
choices: A reframe with real substance
A much longer pitch
An instant discount offer
items.explanation: Substance follows once you know what you are answering.

items.prompt: Which row contains the budget-or-value fork?
choices: "It's not the right time"
"It's too expensive"
"We need to think about it"
items.explanation: The price row is where a budget limit and a value gap can look the same.

items.prompt: A buyer says "it's not the right time." Rep one asks when would be better and waits. Rep two asks if timing is the only thing in the way. After three months, which deal has more likely progressed?
choices: Rep two's, since a hidden blocker was named early
Rep one's, since the buyer was never pressed
Neither, since a timing objection always ends a deal
Rep one's, provided the rep follows up often
items.explanation: Waiting for a fixed later date postpones a blocker that rep two's question brought out while the conversation was live.
items.reference:
Weak versus strong, row by row
"Too expensive": weak caves, strong asks budget or value
"Something that works": weak argues, strong asks what still costs
"Think about it": weak waits, strong asks what to think through
"Not the right time": weak reschedules, strong asks if timing is the only blocker
Why: the strong reply validates the position and asks one specific question; it never argues the buyer out of it.
items.learnMore:
Reading the table

Each weak reply accepts the stated reason at face value or fights it. Each strong reply keeps the buyer's reason on the table and asks a question that either confirms it or surfaces the true one.

Common mistake

Treating "when would be better?" as isolating. It is scheduling.
items.reflection: Pick an objection you often hear at work. What is your weak reply, and what is a strong one in your own words?

items.prompt: Which strong reply best fits "we already have something that works" from a skeptical operations lead?
choices: "Our tool is faster, cheaper and better supported than yours is."
"Most teams like yours end up switching within their first year or so."
"Fair, switching has real costs. Does anything still cost you time?"
"Can I send over a feature comparison sheet for your review?"
items.explanation: It respects switching costs and asks for the buyer's own evidence; the others argue, predict or hand over a document.

items.prompt: A rep drafts "I understand, but..." followed by a rebuttal. What is the problem?
choices: The acknowledgement only leads into an argument
The acknowledgement is longer than it needs to be
The rebuttal contains too many facts for one reply
It should have opened with the price instead of a pause
items.explanation: A "but" after a token acknowledgement signals the rep did not mean it, so the buyer defends as before.

items.prompt: What does anchoring describe?
choices: Writing the price down on a quote
The first number pulling the talk toward it
Holding the price completely fixed for months
items.explanation: Whoever names a number first sets the frame.

items.prompt: A buyer opens with "can you do 20% off?" What is that?
choices: An agreement to the list price
A decision to walk away
An anchor
items.explanation: The buyer is setting the first number.

items.prompt: What should a counter-offer include?
choices: A number plus the reasoning behind it
Only a slightly smaller discount than asked
Only a firm deadline for the buyer
items.explanation: Reasons reset the frame instead of just haggling down.

items.prompt: What does a one-way discount invite?
choices: Longer contracts from the buyer
More requests next time
Smaller orders from the buyer
items.explanation: It teaches the buyer that the price was never fixed.

items.prompt: When is walking away reasonable?
choices: Whenever the buyer says no even once
Never, because every deal matters a great deal
When the concession would cost more than the deal is worth
items.explanation: Some deals are not worth doing.

items.prompt: What should you leave open when you walk away?
choices: The relationship
The price
The contract
items.explanation: A polite no leaves room for a later deal.

items.prompt: When is it best to decide a walk-away limit?
choices: After signing the deal
Before the call
During the buyer's pause

choices: A shorter notice period for leaving
A larger discount at the next renewal
A reference or a longer term
items.explanation: Both items add something of value to the deal.

items.prompt: A buyer says "I need 20% off." The seller replies "14% is where the numbers work, and here is what it covers." What has the seller done?
choices: Conceded the buyer's full anchor without any discussion at all
Countered with a number and reasons, resetting the frame
Refused to negotiate any change to the price
Raised the price above its original list level
items.explanation: A reasoned number gives the buyer something to evaluate instead of a bare haggling step from their own anchor.
items.reference:
Three negotiation mechanics
🔁 Trade, don't give: concessions earn something back
⚓ Anchor with reasons: a number plus why
🚪 Know your walk-away: some deals cost too much
Why: each mechanic works because the trade is explicit and both sides can see what they receive.
items.learnMore:
Why decide the walk-away early

A limit set before the call is easier to hold than one invented under pressure. A deal needing a concession so large that it stops being profitable, or that sets a precedent, is better declined with the door left open.

Common mistake

Treating every lost deal as a failure and conceding to avoid it.
items.reflection: Think of a deal, purchase or agreement you walked away from. What limit did you set, and did you set it before or during the conversation?

Accept, but keep the terms hidden from other customers
Offer an even bigger discount so the deal closes fast
Decline politely and propose a placeholder for later
items.explanation: The deal is below the limit and risks a precedent, so declining while keeping the door open beats closing.

$18,000 a year
$19,800 a year

items.prompt: What budget did Marcus have approved?
choices: About $24,000
About $18,000
About $10,000
items.explanation: He could approve about $18,000 without involving finance.

items.prompt: What did Dana ask for in return for $19,800?
choices: A one-year term and a case study write-up
Full payment up front, a year in advance
A two-year term and a reference call
items.explanation: She traded the price for a longer term and a future reference.

items.prompt: How much did Dana give up per year?
What did Theo's $18,000 come with?
choices: A two-year term and a lock
Nothing asked in return
A reference call from Marcus
items.explanation: He conceded the full $6,000 with no return.

items.prompt: How much did each double-booking cost Marcus?
choices: About $8,400
About $24,000
About $2,100
items.explanation: $2,100 each, four times this quarter.

items.prompt: What did Dana restate to counter-anchor?
choices: The cost Marcus had named
Her own commission rate on the deal
Her main competitor's current price
items.explanation: She rooted the number in Marcus's figure.

items.prompt: What did the locked rate protect against?
choices: A defect in the dispatch product
A list price increase in year two
A late payment by the buyer in year one
items.explanation: The lock held the price steady over two years.

items.prompt: Marcus's cost is 4 incidents a quarter at $2,100. Assuming the rate holds, what is the yearly cost, and how does it compare with the $19,800 price?
choices: $8,400 a year, well below the price
$33,600 a year, about 3 times the price
$33,600 a year, about 1.7 times the price
$25,200 a year, about 1.3 times the price
items.explanation: 4 x 2,100 = 8,400 a quarter, so 33,600 a year; 33,600 / 19,800 is about 1.7. The rate holding is an assumption.
items.reference:
Dana's deal against Theo's
List: $24,000 a year, 1 year
Dana: $19,800 ($4,200 off, 17.5%), 2 years locked, plus a reference
Theo: $18,000 ($6,000 off, 25%), 1 year, nothing back
Marcus's cost: 4 x $2,100 = $8,400 a quarter
Why: Dana gave less, got two things back, and tied the number to a cost Marcus had named.
items.learnMore:
Why $19,800 beat $18,000

The $18,000 was what Marcus could approve without a finance meeting, not an absolute ceiling. Reasoning tied to his own cost, plus a locked two-year rate, made a slightly higher number a better deal over time.

Common mistake

Assuming a budget figure is a hard limit without checking how it was set.
items.reflection: Think of a number you gave in a discussion. Was it tied to something the other person had already said, or only to your own wish?

items.prompt: What is a smokescreen objection?
choices: A reason that is completely true and complete
A stated reason covering a different real blocker
A request for a much bigger discount
items.explanation: The opening line does not match what is really in the way.

items.prompt: What did the director variant need?
choices: A bigger discount on price
A longer product demo
A concrete summary for the director
items.explanation: The real blocker was approval, so the answer is an approval artifact.

items.prompt: What kind of constraint was the frozen category?
choices: A hard limit outside Dana's leverage
A number that reasoning could still move
A negotiating bluff made by Marcus
items.explanation: No trade could change a freeze set elsewhere.

items.prompt: What is the better close for a frozen budget?
choices: A deeper discount to force a yes
A placeholder for when the freeze lifts
A threat to leave the relationship for good
items.explanation: It keeps the relationship open without forcing a sale.

items.prompt: Does walking away mean the method failed?
choices: Yes, in every single case
Only when the buyer is being rude
No, it surfaced that nothing can close
items.explanation: Learning the truth is the method working.

items.prompt: Which question moves a smokescreen forward?
choices: "What would your director want to know?"
"Why do you even need a director to sign?"
"Can you just sign without them this week?"
items.explanation: It turns a vague stall into a concrete step.

items.prompt: Why must isolate run every time?
choices: Buyers forget what they said earlier on
The same opening line can hide different blockers
Company policy requires it on every call made
items.explanation: Two rows in the table share a line but not a cause.

items.prompt: Should Dana spend margin on a deal that cannot close this cycle?
choices: Yes, to build goodwill with the buyer
Yes, in every similar situation
No, it would not change the outcome
items.explanation: A frozen budget makes extra concessions pointless.

items.prompt: Marcus answers the isolate question with "nothing costs us, I just need my director's sign-off." What should Dana do?
choices: Argue even harder that the spreadsheet is really flawed
Offer a discount so that the director can be skipped over
Close the call and wait for a callback
Ask what the director needs to see, then supply it
items.explanation: The stated reason was a smokescreen for approval authority, so the next question is about the director's needs.
items.reference:
Same opening line, different blockers
"Something that works" -> costly double-bookings: point at the capability
"Something that works" -> needs director approval: give the director a summary
"Too expensive" -> $18,000 approval line: counter and trade
"Too expensive" -> frozen category: walk away, keep the door open
Why: isolate must run every time, because the first line does not tell you which blocker is behind it.
items.learnMore:
When the method says stop

A smokescreen needs a second, deeper isolate question about what the decision-maker needs. A frozen budget is a constraint set where the seller has no leverage, so trading harder only spends margin.

Common mistake

Pitching harder at a concern the buyer never had.
items.reflection: Think of a time you accepted a polite reason that turned out to hide another. What question would have shown it earlier?
